items.stem: Two sessions both read one free seat, with no transaction. Both pass the check and both write. How many enrollments exist at the end?

options.text: Two, so the seat is sold twice.
options.feedback: Both sessions read 1 before either one wrote, so both believed a seat was free.

options.text: One, because the database stops the second session.
options.feedback: Nothing stops the second session. The database does not know that the two sessions are competing for the same seat.

options.text: One, because the second write fails when no seat is left.
options.feedback: The write sets the seat count to 0 whatever the current value is, so it does not fail.

options.text: Zero, because the two sessions cancel each other.
options.feedback: Neither session is undone. Both record an enrollment.

items.stem: A developer wraps the same statements in a transaction and expects the problem to disappear. What happens?

options.text: Both sessions can still read 1 and enroll twice.
options.feedback: A transaction groups statements into one unit, but at the default isolation level it does not lock the row.

options.text: The database stops the second session from enrolling.
options.feedback: Both sessions already read 1 before either one wrote, so both go ahead. Holding the row for the whole decision takes a lock.

options.text: The database undoes the second enrollment automatically.
options.feedback: The database undoes work only after an error. Nothing is wrong with the second session's statements.

options.text: Only one session can open a transaction on a table at a time.
options.feedback: Many sessions can have transactions open at once.

items.stem: Which fix lets the second student find out that the seat is gone, without a separate lock?

options.text: Put the check inside the change, then read the rows changed.
options.feedback: The check and the change happen together, so there is no gap. A row count of 0 tells the second student that the seat is gone.

options.text: Lock the row before deciding, so the other session waits for you.
options.feedback: This also works, but the second session waits for the first to finish. The question asks for a fix without a lock.

options.text: Read the seat count twice before writing the new value.
options.feedback: A second read still leaves a gap between reading and writing. Another session can write in that gap.

options.text: Add more web servers so each session has its own copy.
options.feedback: More web servers add more sessions that read the same row. The seat is contested in the database.

items.stem: A save returns successfully and then the server loses power. After the restart, the enrollment is still in the table. Which guarantee made that happen?

options.feedback: Durability means a saved change has been written to disk and survives a power failure.
Atomicity means all of a transaction's statements happen or none do. It does not cover power failures after the save.
Consistency means declared rules stay true. It does not decide whether a change survives a restart.
Isolation controls what sessions see of each other's work while they run. It has nothing to do with restarts.
